title: Thomas's Religion and the Decline of Magic: Foundation of Modern Social History of Witchcraft
description: Keith Thomas published Religion and the Decline of Magic: Studies in Popular Beliefs in Sixteenth and Seventeenth Century England in 1971, a landmark of social history that set the agenda for the modern scholarly study of witchcraft. Drawing on an enormous range of sources, Thomas argued that witch belief was functionally coherent — intelligible as a response to misfortune in a pre-scientific world — and that its decline was connected to the rise of new institutions (insurance, medicine, improved agriculture) that displaced the need for magical explanations. Thomas's charity-refusal model for witch accusation — a person denies charity to a poor neighbor, feels guilt when the neighbor curses them and something goes wrong, and relieves guilt by accusing the neighbor of witchcraft — became foundational.
historiographical_note: Thomas's influence on subsequent witchcraft historiography is difficult to overstate. His functionalist approach was developed by Macfarlane, criticized by Stuart Clark (who argued it ignored intellectual history), and refined by many subsequent scholars. The charity-refusal model was accepted as broadly correct for England while being questioned for its applicability in other regions. Thomas's work exemplifies the 'rationality within framework' principle central to the WitchcraftStudiesDB historiographical approach.
source_method: Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971); subsequent scholarship engaging with Thomas's framework
